newsitem.title: UK: Strong stg no substitute for rate rise - George.
newsitem.headline: Strong stg no substitute for rate rise - George.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Tuesday that the sharp appreciation of sterling through the autumn "should help to dampen inflation at least in the short term".
But in a speech to the Confederation of British Industry here, he added:
"There cannot be any automatic offset against interest rates -- certainly no simple rule of thumb. Nor can the exchange rate become an excuse for over-riding the inflation target."
Sterling has risen by around nine percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August. George said sterling's continued strength was "uncertain".

Rejecting suggestions that the strength of sterling made further rate rises unnecessary, the governor said the rise in the pound "does nothing directly to restrain the domestically-driven upswing in demand.

"We take the view that, while there is still no doubt some degree of spare capacity in the economy, the accelerating upswing will need to moderate if it is not to put the inflation target at risk further ahead," he said.
"That is why we welcomed the recent modest rise in interest rates," he added.
Repeating the view the Bank expressed in last week's quarterly inflation report, George said: "It may well be that some further rise will become necessary in due course."

George said that by acting promptly in raising UK base rates by a quarter point to six percent on October 30, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke had helped to limit "the extent of the rise that may ultimately become necessary, and improved the prospect of expansion."

Turning to the prospects for European Monetary Union (EMU), George said the economic case for EMU depended on whether different member countries found that a single monetary policy and a single interest rate were "at least broadly compatible with their economic situation" on a consistent basis.
"If it worked well in this respect then there would be real advantage in terms of intra-regional exchange rate certainty in a single currency, as well as lower transaction costs."

But if the economic needs of countries diverged in a major way, so that the single interest rate was too expansionary in some and too deflationary in others "that could give rise to serious tensions, including possible persistently higher unemployment in some areas and pressure for protection.
"In that case it would be better for everyone if we all continued to pursue stability-oriented macro-economic policies and structural flexibility independently outside monetary union."
